m1s1p1: The sun delivers more energy to Earth in one hour than all of humanity consumes in an entire year. Capturing even a tiny fraction of that energy can power homes, businesses and entire cities — without burning a single gram of fossil fuel.
m1s1p2: Solar photovoltaic (PV) systems convert sunlight directly into electricity using semiconducting materials. They have no moving parts, produce zero emissions during operation, and their cost has dropped more than 90 % over the last decade.
m1s1callout: Key insight. In 2024, solar PV generated over 6 % of global electricity — up from less than 0.1 % in 2010. The energy transition is already underway.

m1s2p1: The sun produces energy through nuclear fusion — hydrogen atoms merge to form helium, releasing enormous amounts of energy as electromagnetic radiation. That radiation travels 150 million km to reach Earth in about 8 minutes.
m1s2p2: At the top of Earth's atmosphere, the solar irradiance is approximately 1 361 W/m² (the "solar constant"). By the time sunlight reaches sea level a clear-sky peak value of about 1 000 W/m² is the standard used in panel ratings.
m1s2callout: Standard Test Conditions (STC). Panel manufacturers rate their products at 1 000 W/m² irradiance, 25 °C cell temperature and AM 1.5 spectrum. Real-world output is almost always lower.
m1s3p1: Two measurements describe how much solar energy is available at a site:
m1s3li1: Irradiance (W/m²) — the instantaneous power of sunlight falling on a surface.
m1s3li2: Insolation (kWh/m²/day) — the total energy received over a full day. Also called "peak sun hours".
m1s3li3: Tilt & orientation — panels facing the equator at an angle roughly equal to local latitude receive the most annual energy.
m1s4p1: A photovoltaic cell is a semiconductor device — usually made of silicon — that produces a small DC voltage when photons of light knock electrons loose. This is the photoelectric effect, first explained by Einstein in 1905.
m1s4li1: A single silicon cell produces ~0.5 V DC.
m1s4li2: Cells are wired in series inside a module (panel) to reach useful voltages (12 V, 24 V, 48 V…).
m1s4li3: Modules are grouped into strings and combined into an array to meet a system's power requirements.
m1s4li4: An inverter converts the DC output into AC electricity for use in homes and the grid.
m1s5Title: A brief history of solar PV
tl1Desc: Edmond Becquerel observes that certain materials produce electricity when exposed to light.
tl2Desc: Bell Labs creates a silicon PV cell with ~6 % efficiency — enough to power small electronics.
tl3Desc: Rising oil prices push governments to invest in renewable energy research, including solar.
tl4Desc: Feed-in tariffs in Germany and Spain trigger the first large-scale solar boom in Europe.
tl5Title: Solar is the cheapest electricity source
tl5Desc: New utility-scale solar achieves costs below $0.02/kWh in many regions — beating all other generation sources.
